title: The Quiet Truth Beneath the Noise
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Prompted by the death of a member of her Art of Soulful cohort, Kathleen Schafer reflects on leaders who carry a great deal quietly and rarely ask for care in return. She focuses on those who serve the public good, whose work is meaningful but draining, and asks why a culture expects the carers to have fewer supports and less rest than those serving profit. She ties the point to Step Three of her Leadership Connection Model, Alignment of Purpose, which asks leaders to attend to physical, mental, emotional and spiritual state so that care becomes reciprocal. The piece ends with reflection questions inviting readers to notice who around them is giving without receiving.
points: Many of the most dependable leaders carry heavy loads quietly, and their own needs become secondary to service.
For people serving the public good the meaning of the work does not cancel its cost, and care cannot flow in only one direction.
Alignment of Purpose in the Leadership Connection Model frames attention to body, mind, emotion and spirit as staying true to one's life, not self-improvement.
The author asks whether caregivers should be recognized as especially deserving of care.
quotes: There are people who carry a great deal and do not make much noise about it. They show up, serve, lead, tend, uplift, and hold things together, and they help a room feel less alone simply by being in it.
The work is meaningful. It is also draining. The meaning does not cancel the cost, and relationships cannot thrive in only one direction.

I find myself asking how we came to accept a culture where those who care for others are so often the least cared for, where the people who serve the public good are asked to do it with fewer supports and less rest than those whose work serves profit. What I am sensing, underneath those questions, is grief.
A life of service cannot be sustained by neglecting the one who serves. Care has to become reciprocal if it is going to be whole.

So perhaps today, beneath the noise of summer, we might listen differently, not for what needs to get done, but for the quieter truth that has been asking for care. What would change if those who care for others were recognized as especially deserving of care themselves?
